summary: T'UKRI is a web platform that brings together thermal anomaly detections from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS sensors to help users explore and compare hot spot data. Its interactive map and time-based views organize observations by location, date, sensor, and confidence. For the current prototype, focused on Huánuco, Peru, the platform adds MapBiomas land-cover data to help screen observations and identify possible fire events for further review. It also preserves each detection’s source and evaluation details so users can understand how results were categorized. T'UKRI supports more informed monitoring of potential fires, while making clear that a satellite thermal anomaly alone does not confirm a fire or its cause.
details:
🧑‍🚒 T'UKRI is a web platform for exploring and adding context to thermal anomalies detected by NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS sensors. The current prototype focuses on Huánuco, Peru, in 2026, and uses MapBiomas Peru Collection 4 land-cover data from 2025 as a reference for evaluating the areas around detections.

How It Works

The platform displays observations on an interactive map and in time-based views. It preserves information such as each observation’s source, sensor, and confidence level. Transparent rules also organize possible events that may need attention, cases requiring review, and detections excluded from the main view based on their characteristics.

Benefits and Expected Impact

T'UKRI aims to help researchers, public agencies, and monitoring teams review large volumes of thermal data and prioritize areas for further assessment. By combining detections with territorial context, it supports analysis that is more informed and easier to understand.

💻 Technology Stack

  • Frontend: Vue 3, TypeScript, and Vite.
  • Mapping and visualization: MapLibre GL and ECharts.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Geospatial database: PostgreSQL and PostGIS.
  • Data sources: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS) and MapBiomas Peru layers.

Github Link

Innovation Highlights

  • Brings MODIS and VIIRS observations into a shared experience for exploring and comparing data.
  • Adds land-cover context to support the evaluation of detections.
  • Preserves traceability of each observation’s source and the criteria used to classify it.
  • Organizes possible events and cases for review without presenting detections as confirmed fires.

Factors Considered

The team considered data provenance and quality, differences between sensors, temporal and geographic coverage, map-layer resolution, and the risk of assigning a cause to a thermal anomaly without additional evidence. MapBiomas 2025 is used as a reference for 2026 detections, so it may not represent land cover at the time of each observation.
